title: The Genitive Absolute
subtitle: ταῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ Κύρου — an independent participial phrase.
objectives: Understand the genitive absolute as a participial phrase grammatically independent of the main sentence.
Translate genitive absolutes into natural English temporal or causal clauses.
Recognize when a participle is in the genitive absolute versus when it agrees with a noun in the main sentence.
Use the genitive absolute to express time, cause, or circumstance.

sections.heading: The genitive absolute
sections.body:
The genitive absolute is a participial phrase in the genitive case, grammatically independent of the main sentence. It consists of a noun (or pronoun) in the genitive and a participle agreeing with it in the genitive.

ταῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ Κύρου, ἀνέστησαν οἱ στρατιῶται.
'These things having been said by Cyrus' or 'When Cyrus had said these things, the soldiers stood up.'

ταῦτα is the object of the participle εἰπόντος (aorist active participle of λέγω, genitive singular masculine). τοῦ Κύρου is the subject of the participle, also in the genitive. The whole phrase is in the genitive because it is independent of the main sentence.

sections.heading: When to use the genitive absolute
sections.body:
The genitive absolute is used when the subject of the participle is different from the subject of the main verb. If the subject of the participle is the same as the subject of the main verb, use a circumstantial participle in the same case as the subject, not a genitive absolute.

Correct: ταῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ Κύρου, ἀνέστησαν οἱ στρατιῶται.
Cyrus is the subject of εἰπόντος; the soldiers are the subject of ἀνέστησαν. Different subjects → genitive absolute.

Incorrect: *οἱ στρατιῶται εἰπόντες ταῦτα ἀνέστησαν.
This would mean 'The soldiers, having said these things, stood up.' But if the soldiers are the subject of both the participle and the main verb, use a nominative participle, not a genitive absolute.

sections.heading: Translating the genitive absolute
sections.body:
The genitive absolute is usually translated as a temporal, causal, or concessive clause in English.

Temporal: 'when X happened', 'after X happened', 'while X was happening'
Causal: 'because X happened', 'since X happened'
Concessive: 'although X happened'

Context tells you which is most natural.

ταῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ Κύρου → 'When Cyrus had said these things' or 'After Cyrus said these things'.

τούτων πραττομένων → 'While these things were being done' or 'Since these things were being done'.

sections.heading: From Xenophon
sections.body:
Anabasis I.1.2: ταῦτα πράξαντος τοῦ Κύρου, ἀνέστησαν οἱ Ἕλληνες.
'When Cyrus had done these things, the Greeks stood up.' ταῦτα πράξαντος τοῦ Κύρου is a genitive absolute: Cyrus is the subject of πράξαντος, the Greeks are the subject of ἀνέστησαν.

items.answer: A participial phrase in the genitive case, grammatically independent of the main sentence.

items.prompt: When do you use the genitive absolute?
items.answer: When the subject of the participle is different from the subject of the main verb.

items.prompt: Translate: ταῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ Κύρου, ἀνέστησαν οἱ στρατιῶται.
items.answer: When Cyrus had said these things, the soldiers stood up.
While these things were being done

items.prompt: Can you use a genitive absolute when the subject of the participle is the same as the subject of the main verb?
items.answer: No. Use a circumstantial participle in the same case as the subject.
